solution:
Let the object-screen distance be \(D = 3\,\text{m}\) and let the lens stand a distance \(x\) from the bulb, so the screen is at \(D - x\). For a real image both distances are positive, and the lens equation becomes

\(\dfrac{1}{D - x} + \dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)

\(\dfrac{D}{x(D - x)} = \dfrac{1}{f} \quad\Rightarrow\quad x^{2} - Dx + Df = 0\)

A lens position exists only if this quadratic has a real root, i.e. if its discriminant is non-negative:

\(D^{2} - 4Df \ge 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad f \le \dfrac{D}{4}\)

So the largest focal length that can still throw a real image across the room is

\(f_{max} = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75\,\text{m}\)

Maximum possible focal length \(= 0.75\,\text{m}\) (\(75\,\text{cm}\)).

This is the displacement (conjugate-foci) method. With the object and screen a fixed distance \(D\) apart, the two lens positions that give a sharp image are the two roots of \(x^{2} - Dx + Df = 0\), and their separation is

\(d = |x_1 - x_2| = \sqrt{D^{2} - 4Df}\)

Solving for \(f\):

\(d^{2} = D^{2} - 4Df \quad\Rightarrow\quad f = \dfrac{D^{2} - d^{2}}{4D}\)

With \(D = 90\,\text{cm}\) and \(d = 20\,\text{cm}\):

\(f = \dfrac{90^{2} - 20^{2}}{4 \times 90} = \dfrac{8100 - 400}{360} = \dfrac{7700}{360} = 21.4\,\text{cm}\)

Focal length of the lens \(= 21.4\,\text{cm}\).

The lenses of Exercise 9.10 are \(f_1 = +30\,\text{cm}\) (convex) and \(f_2 = -20\,\text{cm}\) (concave), now \(8.0\,\text{cm}\) apart. Because they are NOT in contact, the powers cannot simply be added; each lens must be handled in turn.

(a) (i) Parallel light striking the CONVEX lens first. \(u_1 = -\infty\) gives \(v_1 = +30\,\text{cm}\). That image lies \(30 - 8 = 22\,\text{cm}\) beyond the concave lens, so it is a virtual object for it, \(u_2 = +22\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{-20} + \dfrac{1}{22} = \dfrac{-11 + 10}{220} = -\dfrac{1}{220}\)

\(v_2 = -220\,\text{cm}\)

The emergent beam diverges from a point \(220\,\text{cm}\) to the left of the concave lens, i.e. \(216\,\text{cm}\) from the centre of the two-lens system.

(ii) Parallel light striking the CONCAVE lens first. \(u_1 = -\infty\) gives \(v_1 = -20\,\text{cm}\), which is \(20 + 8 = 28\,\text{cm}\) to the left of the convex lens, a real object \(u_2 = -28\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{28} = \dfrac{28 - 30}{840} = -\dfrac{1}{420}\)

\(v_2 = -420\,\text{cm}\), i.e. \(416\,\text{cm}\) from the centre of the system.

The two answers differ, so YES, the result depends on which face the light enters. Because no single number reproduces the behaviour from both sides, there is no constant of the system playing the role of a focal length: the notion of an 'effective focal length' is not meaningful for this arrangement.

(b) Object \(1.5\,\text{cm}\) tall, \(40\,\text{cm}\) from the convex lens. First lens:

\(\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{1}{120} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_1 = 120\,\text{cm}\), and \(|m_1| = \dfrac{120}{40} = 3\)

This image is \(120 - 8 = 112\,\text{cm}\) past the concave lens, a virtual object \(u_2 = +112\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{-20} + \dfrac{1}{112} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_2 = -\dfrac{112 \times 20}{92} = -24.35\,\text{cm}\)

\(|m_2| = \left|\dfrac{v_2}{u_2}\right| = \dfrac{20}{92} = 0.217\)

Net magnification \(= |m_1||m_2| = 3 \times 0.217 = 0.652\)

Size of image \(= 0.652 \times 1.5 = 0.98\,\text{cm}\)

(a) The beam appears to diverge from \(216\,\text{cm}\) (convex first) or \(416\,\text{cm}\) (concave first) from the centre of the system; the answer DOES depend on the side, and an effective focal length is not a useful notion here.
(b) Magnification \(= 0.652\); size of the image \(= 0.98\,\text{cm}\).

"Just suffers total internal reflection at the other face" means the ray reaches the second face exactly at the critical angle, so \(r_2 = i_c\).

\(\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1.524} = 0.6562 \quad\Rightarrow\quad i_c = 41^\circ\)

For a prism, \(r_1 + r_2 = A\), so

\(r_1 = 60^\circ - 41^\circ = 19^\circ\)

Applying Snell's law at the first face:

\(\sin i = n \sin r_1 = 1.524 \times \sin 19^\circ = 1.524 \times 0.3256 = 0.4962\)

\(i = \sin^{-1}(0.4962) = 29.7^\circ\)

The ray must be incident at about \(30^\circ\) on the first face.

The card is at \(u = -9\,\text{cm}\) from a converging lens of focal length \(f = 10\,\text{cm}\), viewed with the eye close to the lens; the near point is \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\).

(a) Lens equation:

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{9 - 10}{90} = -\dfrac{1}{90}\)

\(v = -90\,\text{cm}\) — a virtual image on the same side as the card.

\(|m| = \left|\dfrac{v}{u}\right| = \dfrac{90}{9} = 10\)

Area scales as the SQUARE of the linear magnification, so each square becomes

\(10 \times 10 \times 1 = 100\,\text{mm}^{2} = 1\,\text{cm}^{2}\)

(b) Angular magnification of a simple magnifier used this way is set by how much closer than the near point the object can be brought:

\(\text{MP} = \dfrac{D}{|u|} = \dfrac{25}{9} = 2.8\)

(c) NO — they are different quantities and they happen to differ here. Linear magnification \(|v/u|\) compares the physical SIZE of image and object. Angular magnification compares the angle the image subtends at the eye with the angle the object would subtend if placed at the near point, and equals \(D/|u|\). They coincide only when the image itself is formed at the near point, i.e. \(|v| = 25\,\text{cm}\); here \(|v| = 90\,\text{cm}\), so \(10 \ne 2.8\).

(a) \(|m| = 10\); each square has area \(100\,\text{mm}^{2} = 1\,\text{cm}^{2}\) in the virtual image.
(b) Magnifying power \(= 2.8\).
(c) No — the two are equal only when the image is at the near point.
_note: BOOK DEFECT (stem). The printed stem gives BOTH the viewing distance AND the focal length as 9 cm — verified on the page at 5x magnification. As printed the object sits exactly at the focus, so v is infinite and part (a) has no answer at all. Solved with f = 10 cm, which is what the book's own answers require, on THREE independent counts: 9.22's key writes '1/v + 1/9 = 1/10'; 9.23's key value u = -7.14 cm reproduces only with f = 10 (f = 9 would give -6.62 cm); and 9.24's key prints the equation '1/(2.5u) - 1/u = 1/10' literally. So 'focal length 9 cm' should read 'focal length 10 cm'. Ex 9.23 and Ex 9.24 both refer back to this lens and inherit the defect.

solution:
The lens of Exercise 9.22 has \(f = 10\,\text{cm}\); the near point is \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\).

(a) A simple magnifier gives its greatest angular magnification when the eye is working hardest, i.e. when the virtual image is formed right at the near point, \(v = -25\,\text{cm}\).

\(\dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{f} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -0.14\)

\(u = -7.14\,\text{cm}\)

So the lens is held \(7.14\,\text{cm}\) from the card sheet.

(b) \(|m| = \left|\dfrac{v}{u}\right| = \dfrac{25}{7.14} = 3.5\)

(c) Magnifying power \(= \dfrac{D}{|u|} = \dfrac{25}{7.14} = 3.5\) — equivalently \(1 + \dfrac{D}{f} = 1 + 2.5 = 3.5\).

YES, they are equal in this case, and for the reason identified in Exercise 9.22: the two quantities agree exactly when the image is formed at the near point, which is the condition imposed in part (a).

(a) The lens should be held \(7.14\,\text{cm}\) from the sheet.
(b) Magnification \(= 3.5\).
(c) Magnifying power \(= 3.5\) — yes, equal, because the image is at the near point.
_note: Inherits the Ex 9.22 stem defect: solved with f = 10 cm (the printed 9 cm makes Ex 9.22 degenerate). The key's own u = -7.14 cm confirms f = 10.

solution:
Each square is \(1\,\text{mm}^{2}\) and its virtual image is to be \(6.25\,\text{mm}^{2}\). Area goes as the square of the linear magnification, so

\(|m| = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.25}{1}} = 2.5\)

The image is virtual and erect, on the same side as the object, so \(v = 2.5u\). With \(f = 10\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2.5u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10}\)

\(\dfrac{1 - 2.5}{2.5u} = \dfrac{1}{10} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{-1.5}{2.5u} = \dfrac{1}{10} \quad\Rightarrow\quad u = -6\,\text{cm}\)

\(|v| = 2.5 \times 6 = 15\,\text{cm}\)

The image lies only \(15\,\text{cm}\) from the eye, which is CLOSER than the near point of \(25\,\text{cm}\). A normal eye cannot focus that close, so although the squares are magnified they will not be seen distinctly.

The object must be \(6\,\text{cm}\) from the magnifying glass. No — the virtual image forms at \(15\,\text{cm}\), inside the near point, so the squares cannot be seen distinctly with the eye close to the magnifier.
_note: Inherits the Ex 9.22 stem defect: solved with f = 10 cm. The key here literally prints the equation '1/(2.5u) - 1/u = 1/10', i.e. f = 10.

solution:
The premise is correct: with the eye close to the lens, the virtual image does subtend the same angle at the eye as the object itself does. The gain does not come from that comparison.

What the magnifier buys is the ability to bring the object MUCH CLOSER than the eye could otherwise tolerate. Unaided, the nearest an object can be held and still be seen sharply is the near point, about \(25\,\text{cm}\); at that distance an object of height \(h\) subtends only \(h/25\). With the magnifier the object can be placed at roughly its focal length — a few centimetres — and the eye still receives a beam it can focus, because the lens throws the image far away.

Angular magnification is defined as the ratio of these two angles:

\(\text{MP} = \dfrac{\text{angle subtended with the magnifier}}{\text{angle subtended by the object at the near point}} = \dfrac{h/|u|}{h/D} = \dfrac{D}{|u|}\)

Since \(|u| \ll D\), this ratio is large.

So the magnification is achieved by allowing a much smaller object distance, not by the image subtending a larger angle than the object at the same place.

Yes — it decreases a little.

With the eye touching the lens, every ray leaving the lens towards the image also passes the eye, so the angle subtended at the eye equals the angle subtended at the lens. Move the eye back and it is no longer at the vertex of that cone: the image, being at a finite distance, now subtends a slightly SMALLER angle at the eye than it does at the lens, so the angular magnification falls.

The effect is negligible when the image is very far away (in the limit of an image at infinity the rays reaching the eye from a given object point are parallel, so the angle is the same wherever the eye is placed).

Moving back also costs field of view, since the eye then accepts light from a narrower cone of the lens aperture.

So angular magnification decreases slightly as the eye is moved back, the decrease being negligible for a distant image.

Two things stop us, one practical and one optical.

First, a very short focal length demands strongly curved surfaces, and grinding and polishing a lens to a very small radius of curvature accurately is difficult.

Second and more important, ABERRATIONS grow rapidly as the focal length is reduced. Both spherical aberration (rays through the rim focusing at a different point from paraxial rays) and chromatic aberration (different colours focusing at different points) become severe, so the image degrades faster than the magnification improves — there is no gain in magnifying a blur.

In practice these limit a single convex lens to a magnifying power of about 3. Using an aberration-corrected combination of lenses instead of one simple lens, the limit can be pushed up by roughly a factor of 10.

So the limit is set by manufacturing difficulty and, decisively, by aberrations — not by the formula \(\text{MP} \propto 1/f\) itself.

Both stages of the magnification improve as their focal lengths shrink.

EYEPIECE. It works as a simple magnifier, with angular magnification

\(m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e} \quad (D = 25\,\text{cm})\)

which clearly increases as \(f_e\) is made smaller.

OBJECTIVE. Its linear magnification can be written

\(m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|} = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{|u_o|}{f_o}\right) - 1}\)

which is large only when \(|u_o|\) is just a little greater than \(f_o\). A microscope is used on objects placed very close to the objective, so \(|u_o|\) is necessarily small — and for \(|u_o|\) to sit just above \(f_o\), \(f_o\) must be smaller still.

So a short \(f_e\) makes the eyepiece a strong magnifier, and a short \(f_o\) is forced by the requirement that the object sit just outside the objective's focus; both are therefore kept short.

The eyepiece forms an image of the OBJECTIVE, and this small bright disc is called the eye-ring. Every ray that the objective collects and sends into the eyepiece must pass through the eye-ring, so it is the one place where the eye can intercept all of the light the instrument has gathered.

If the eye is pressed right against the eyepiece it sits in front of the eye-ring: it then misses some of the refracted light and, because it accepts a narrower cone from the eyepiece, it also loses field of view. Placing the pupil ON the eye-ring — with the pupil at least as large as the ring — collects the whole beam and gives the widest field.

The eye-ring lies a short way beyond the eyepiece, and its exact position follows from the separation between the objective and the eyepiece, so it differs from instrument to instrument. It is not a quantity the user has to compute: in a real microscope the correct eye-to-eyepiece distance is built into the design of the eyepiece mount.

So the eye should be placed at the eye-ring, the image of the objective formed by the eyepiece; its distance from the eyepiece is fixed by the objective-eyepiece separation and is built into the instrument.

Assume normal use, i.e. the final image at the near point \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\). The total magnifying power is the product of the two stages.

Eyepiece:

\(m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e} = 1 + \dfrac{25}{5} = 6\)

So the objective must supply

\(m_o = \dfrac{30}{6} = 5\)

For the objective, \(m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\) with the image inverted, so \(v_o = -5u_o\). Substituting in the lens equation with \(f_o = 1.25\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{-5u_o} - \dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{1.25} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{-1.2}{u_o} = 0.8\)

\(u_o = -1.5\,\text{cm}\), and hence \(v_o = 7.5\,\text{cm}\).

Eyepiece object distance, with \(v_e = -25\,\text{cm}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{u_e} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{1}{5} = -0.24 \quad\Rightarrow\quad u_e = -4.17\,\text{cm}\)

The objective's image must land \(4.17\,\text{cm}\) in front of the eyepiece, so the tube length is

\(v_o + |u_e| = 7.5 + 4.17 = 11.67\,\text{cm}\)

Place the object \(1.5\,\text{cm}\) from the objective and separate the objective and eyepiece by \(11.67\,\text{cm}\).

In normal adjustment the final image is at infinity, which happens when the objective's focal plane coincides with the eyepiece's. The magnifying power is then simply the ratio of the focal lengths:

\(m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{140}{5.0} = 28\)

Magnifying power in normal adjustment \(= 28\).

When the final image is brought to the least distance of distinct vision, the eyepiece works as a simple magnifier forming its image at \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\) instead of at infinity, and the magnifying power becomes

\(m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right)\)

With \(f_o = 140\,\text{cm}\), \(f_e = 5.0\,\text{cm}\) and \(D = 25\,\text{cm}\):

\(m = \dfrac{140}{5.0}\left(1 + \dfrac{5.0}{25}\right) = 28 \times 1.2 = 33.6\)

Magnifying power with the final image at \(25\,\text{cm}\) \(= 33.6\).
_note: BOOK DEFECT (in the answer key's working, not its value). The key prints the formula as (f_o/f_e)[1 + f_o/25] — f_o where f_e belongs. As printed that evaluates to 28 x 6.6 = 184.8, which contradicts the key's OWN printed value of 33.6. The correct form (f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/25) gives exactly 33.6, so the value is right and the printed formula is a typo. Self-refuting on the key's own numbers.

solution:
The telescope of Exercise 9.27 has \(f_o = 140\,\text{cm}\) and \(f_e = 5.0\,\text{cm}\).

(a) In normal adjustment the two focal planes coincide, so the tube length is

\(L = f_o + f_e = 140 + 5.0 = 145\,\text{cm}\)

(b) The tower subtends at the objective

\(\theta = \dfrac{100}{3000} = \dfrac{1}{30}\,\text{rad}\)

The objective forms its image in its focal plane, so that image subtends the same angle and has height

\(h = f_o\,\theta = 140 \times \dfrac{1}{30} = 4.7\,\text{cm}\)

(c) The eyepiece then magnifies this intermediate image. With the final image at \(25\,\text{cm}\),

\(m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e} = 1 + \dfrac{25}{5.0} = 6\)

Final image height \(= 4.7 \times 6 = 28\,\text{cm}\)

(a) Separation \(= 145\,\text{cm}\).
(b) Height of the image formed by the objective \(= 4.7\,\text{cm}\).
(c) Height of the final image \(= 28\,\text{cm}\).

Focal lengths from the radii: the large concave (primary) mirror has \(f_1 = R_1/2 = 220/2 = 110\,\text{mm}\), and the small convex (secondary) mirror has \(|f_2| = R_2/2 = 140/2 = 70\,\text{mm}\).

Left alone, the primary would bring the parallel light from the distant object to a focus \(110\,\text{mm}\) in front of itself. But the secondary intercepts the converging beam after only \(20\,\text{mm}\), so that would-be focus lies

\(110 - 20 = 90\,\text{mm}\)

BEYOND the secondary. The light is converging towards it when it strikes the secondary, so it is a VIRTUAL OBJECT for the secondary at \(90\,\text{mm}\).

For the secondary, both this virtual object and its own focus lie on the far side, so

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{70} - \dfrac{1}{90} = \dfrac{9 - 7}{630} = \dfrac{2}{630} = \dfrac{1}{315}\)

\(v = 315\,\text{mm}\)

The convex secondary has made the beam converge more gently, pushing the focus back past the primary and through the hole in it — which is exactly where the eyepiece sits. (Being \(20\,\text{mm}\) from the primary, the secondary puts this image \(315 - 20 = 295\,\text{mm}\) behind the primary.)

The final image is formed \(315\,\text{mm}\) from the smaller (secondary) mirror.

When a plane mirror is turned through an angle \(\theta\) while the incident ray stays fixed, the normal turns through \(\theta\) and the reflected ray turns through \(2\theta\) — the standard result behind the lamp-and-scale method.

Here \(\theta = 3.5^\circ\), so the reflected ray swings through

\(2\theta = 7.0^\circ\)

The spot on a screen a distance \(L = 1.5\,\text{m}\) away is displaced by

\(d = L\tan 2\theta = 1.5 \times \tan 7.0^\circ = 1.5 \times 0.1228 = 0.184\,\text{m}\)

Displacement of the spot \(= 0.184\,\text{m} = 18.4\,\text{cm}\).

In each trial the needle's inverted image coincides with the needle itself. That happens when the rays strike the plane mirror normally, i.e. when the needle sits at the FOCUS of the optical system above the mirror. So each measured distance is a focal length.

Without the liquid, only the lens is present:

\(f_{lens} = 30.0\,\text{cm}\)

Find its radius of curvature from the lens maker's formula. The lens is equiconvex, so \(R_1 = +R\), \(R_2 = -R\), and with \(n = 1.50\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f_{lens}} = (n - 1)\dfrac{2}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R = f_{lens} = 30.0\,\text{cm}\)

With the liquid present, the liquid layer between the lens and the flat mirror is itself a plano-concave lens, in contact with the glass lens. In contact, focal lengths combine as

\(\dfrac{1}{f_{comb}} = \dfrac{1}{f_{lens}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{liq}}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{45.0} = \dfrac{1}{30.0} + \dfrac{1}{f_{liq}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{f_{liq}} = \dfrac{2 - 3}{90} = -\dfrac{1}{90}\)

\(f_{liq} = -90.0\,\text{cm}\)

The liquid lens has its upper surface moulded against the lens (radius \(R_1 = -30.0\,\text{cm}\), curving away from the incoming light) and a flat lower face on the mirror (\(R_2 = \infty\)):

\(\dfrac{1}{f_{liq}} = (n_{liq} - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{-30.0} - 0\right)\)

\(-\dfrac{1}{90} = -\dfrac{n_{liq} - 1}{30} \quad\Rightarrow\quad n_{liq} - 1 = \dfrac{30}{90} = 0.333\)

Refractive index of the liquid \(= 1.33\).
